slides.title: Average effects describe people; a policy value describes a rule
slides.text: Four summaries you will use all week Average effects describe people; a policy value describes a rule ATE Mean of Y(1) - Y(0) over everyone. ATT The same mean over those who were treated. CATE τ(x): the mean effect for seekers who look like x. Policy value V(π): mean outcome if rule π decided. Q1 is an ATT. Q2 is a policy value under a budget. Q3 compares two policy values.

slides.title: With one place per five seekers, the question becomes a ranking
slides.text: Why the budget matters With one place per five seekers, the question becomes a ranking Treat-all is not on the table: 20% of seekers get a place. The best rule gives places to the largest effects, not the largest needs. A rule's gain is the sum of the effects of the seekers it picks. So the estimand of Q2 needs the CATE, then the value of a rule built from it. 1 in 5 places per job seeker next year

slides.title: Risk is the outcome without coaching; benefit is the difference coaching makes
slides.text: The idea the week turns on Risk is the outcome without coaching; benefit is the difference coaching makes Risk score Predicts Y(0): who will not find work without help. Built to find need. Benefit Y(1) - Y(0): who finds work because of coaching. Small for those who find work anyway, and for those who do not either way. What goes wrong. A model with a high AUC for the outcome says nothing about who benefits. Ranking by it fills places with seekers coaching does not move.

slides.title: The propensity score summarises why a seeker was offered coaching
slides.text: Recap from DS-303 The propensity score summarises why a seeker was offered coaching e(x) = P(offered | x), estimated from the confounders. Given no hidden confounders, comparing seekers with equal e(x) compares like with like. Balance and overlap are checked, never assumed. DS-303, Day 2 Logistic propensity, matching, weighting, trimming and augmented weighting are taught there. Here they run on 60 confounders with flexible models.

slides.title: Positivity: every kind of seeker had some chance of each decision
slides.text: The assumption every method needs Positivity: every kind of seeker had some chance of each decision Where it holds Offered and not offered seekers look alike somewhere: the logs show what coaching did for people like them. Where it fails A group never offered coaching has no offered twin. Any number for them comes from a model's extrapolation. What goes wrong. Weighting divides by e(x). A score of 0.01 makes one decision count like a hundred.

slides.title: Double machine learning
slides.text: Session 3 Double machine learning Explain why plugging machine learning predictions into a regression biases the effect Estimate an average effect with cross-fitting by hand and with a library Report an estimate table with intervals against regression adjustment 03

slides.title: Sixty confounders, and caseworkers who used them in curves and combinations
slides.text: Why the old tools struggle Sixty confounders, and caseworkers who used them in curves and combinations 13 named attributes, the risk score and 46 fields of administrative history. Offers depend on some fields through thresholds and interactions. A linear regression with 60 controls assumes straight lines for all of them. A flexible model fits the curves, but its predictions carry bias of their own. 60 confounders in the logs

slides.title: Plugging machine learning predictions into an effect formula passes their bias straight through
slides.text: The tempting shortcut Plugging machine learning predictions into an effect formula passes their bias straight through Plug-in Fit m1, m0, average m1(x) - m0(x). Regularisation shrinks the models, and the effect shrinks or shifts with them. Same-data fitting Fit and predict on the same rows: residuals look too small, intervals too narrow. Two fixes, together. An orthogonal score so small model errors cancel to first order, and cross-fitting so no decision helps predict itself.

slides.title: The DML score is the augmented weighting score of DS-303, with cross-fitted parts
slides.text: The interactive regression model The DML score is the augmented weighting score of DS-303, with cross-fitted parts psi = (m1 - m0 + t * (y - m1) / e - (1 - t) * (y - m0) / (1 - e)) estimate = psi.mean() se = psi.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n) Outcome models give the first guess. Weighted residuals correct it. Errors in one part are cancelled by the other.

slides.title: Each fold's nuisance predictions come from models fitted on the other folds
slides.text: Cross-fitting, written out Each fold's nuisance predictions come from models fitted on the other folds fold = U.folds(n, 5) for f in range(5): a, b = fold != f, fold == f e[b] = clf().fit(X[a], t[a]).predict_proba(X[b])[:, 1] m1[b] = clf().fit(X[a & (t == 1)], y[a & (t == 1)]).predict_proba(X[b])[:, 1] m0[b] = clf().fit(X[a & (t == 0)], y[a & (t == 0)]).predict_proba(X[b])[:, 1] e = np.clip(e, 0.01, 0.99)

slides.title: DoubleML wraps the folds, the score and the interval in one object
slides.text: The same thing with a library DoubleML wraps the folds, the score and the interval in one object data = dml.DoubleMLData(df, y_col="employed_6m", d_cols="offered", x_cols=list(X.columns)) irm = dml.DoubleMLIRM(data, ml_g=U.gbm_classifier(), ml_m=U.gbm_classifier(), n_folds=5).fit() print(irm.summary) Examples, not endorsements. EconML's LinearDML, CausalML and grf for R estimate the same quantity. Write it by hand once, then use a library you can check.

slides.title: A bound tells you how strong something missing would have to be, not whether it exists
slides.text: Limits A bound tells you how strong something missing would have to be, not whether it exists Ask the people who made the decisions what they saw that the data do not hold. Benchmark against an observed covariate the caseworkers would recognise. Report the robustness value next to the estimate, every time. When the bound is wide, the answer is a randomised trial, which Day 4 designs.

slides.title: Meta-learners
slides.text: Session 1 Meta-learners Fit S-, T- and X-learners on a randomised pilot Explain why an S-learner shrinks effects towards zero Measure each learner against known effects and say why that is impossible on real data 01

slides.title: A randomised pilot removes confounding, so every remaining problem is noise
slides.text: Where heterogeneous effects are learnt A randomised pilot removes confounding, so every remaining problem is noise A lottery within each office: the propensity is 0.5 for everyone. Any group fixed before the lottery can be compared directly. 6,000 seekers, a binary outcome: individual effects are never seen, and groups are noisy. Real programmes Job-search programmes show effects that differ by person; Knaus, Lechner and Strittmatter (2022) estimated them with machine learning on Swiss administrative data.

slides.title: Meta-learners turn a prediction model into an effect estimator
slides.text: Any classifier, three ways Meta-learners turn a prediction model into an effect estimator S-learner One model μ(x, t); effect μ(x,1) - μ(x,0). T-learner Two models, one per arm; effect μ1(x) - μ0(x). X-learner Impute each seeker's effect with the other arm's model, then model the imputed effects.

slides.title: One model with coaching as a feature tends to shrink effects towards zero
slides.text: S-learner One model with coaching as a feature tends to shrink effects towards zero m = clone(BASE).fit(np.column_stack([Xtr, ttr]), ytr) one = np.column_stack([X, np.ones(len(X))]) zero = np.column_stack([X, np.zeros(len(X))]) tau_s = m.predict_proba(one)[:, 1] - m.predict_proba(zero)[:, 1] What goes wrong. Regularised trees split on the strongest predictors of employment. Coaching is one column of nineteen; effects that differ by seeker need splits on coaching inside each branch.

slides.title: Two separate models subtract their errors, and the difference looks like heterogeneity
slides.text: T-learner Two separate models subtract their errors, and the difference looks like heterogeneity What it does well Lets each arm have its own shape; nothing forces effects to be small. What it gets wrong Each model fits noise in its own arm; their difference adds the two noises. 10.5 vs 10.1 spread of T-learner effects against the truth (points, sd)

slides.title: The X-learner models imputed effects, which are smoother than outcomes
slides.text: X-learner The X-learner models imputed effects, which are smoother than outcomes 1 · T-learner μ1, μ0 → 2 · Impute y - μ0(x) for the coached, μ1(x) - y for the others → 3 · Model τ1, τ0 on the imputed effects → 4 · Blend e·τ0 + (1-e)·τ1 In a lottery e = 0.5: the two halves count equally. With unequal arms, the imputations made with the larger arm's model count more.

slides.title: A causal forest splits where the effect changes, not where the outcome changes
slides.text: The causal forest's idea A causal forest splits where the effect changes, not where the outcome changes A prediction tree Splits on months unemployed because employment falls with it. A causal tree Splits on months unemployed only if coaching works differently on each side.

slides.title: Local centring removes the outcome level; honesty keeps the splits from grading themselves
slides.text: Two ingredients Local centring removes the outcome level; honesty keeps the splits from grading themselves Local centring Residualise y and t on x first, as in DML, so splits chase effects, not levels. Honesty Half of each subsample picks the splits; the other half estimates the leaf effects.

slides.title: Individual effects are never observed, so an effect model cannot be scored seeker by seeker
slides.text: The problem Individual effects are never observed, so an effect model cannot be scored seeker by seeker No row has both outcomes: the usual test set metrics do not exist. Groups do have observable effects, if the groups were randomised. So validation compares groups defined by the prediction with their observed effects. Held out and randomised 2,400 pilot seekers the models never saw, coached by the same lottery.

slides.title: Keep the decisions the rule agrees with, and weight each by one over its probability
slides.text: Inverse propensity value Keep the decisions the rule agrees with, and weight each by one over its probability p_a = np.where(a == 1, p, 1 - p) # probability of what the logs did w = (a == rule) / p_a # zero where the rule disagrees value = np.mean(w * y) Recap from DS-303. The same weights estimated an average effect there; a rule's value is the weighted mean outcome under one decision per seeker.

slides.title: Self-normalising tames the weights; augmenting adds an outcome model and keeps the estimate honest
slides.text: Two refinements Self-normalising tames the weights; augmenting adds an outcome model and keeps the estimate honest Self-normalised Divide by the sum of the weights, not by n. A little bias, much less variance. Augmented Start from μ under the rule; add the weighted residual where logs and rule agree. Consistent if either part is right. psi = np.where(rule == 1, mu1, mu0) + w * (y - np.where(a == 1, mu1, mu0))

Predicted and observed effects agree across deciles: correlation above 0.9.

slides.text: Fault 1 A subgroup defined after the lottery is selected, not randomised 3.42 vs 2.50 motivation before the lottery: four or more sessions against fewer Only coached seekers have sessions; no comparable uncoached group exists. slides.title: The largest of 60 cells is mostly the noise that made it the largest

slides.title: Search every pair of splits; keep the tree whose offered seekers have the largest summed gain
slides.text: Policy trees Search every pair of splits; keep the tree whose offered seekers have the largest summed gain Split 1 every allowed attribute, every threshold → Split 2 the best split inside each side → Leaves offer where the summed score beats the cost Unlike a CART tree, it is not greedy: the first split is chosen for what the second makes possible.
